passage.title: Repair and the Public Library
passage.contentNote: Original Cortex practice essay and fictional examples. Independent CARS review is pending. This is not an official AAMC item.
passage.text:
A public library considering a lending collection of household tools faces a deceptively simple question: does a drill belong among books? One critic says that a library preserves recorded thought, whereas a drill merely makes holes. A supporter replies that libraries have always helped people do things, including things that occur beyond a reading room. Both arguments make the decision appear to depend on discovering the institution’s timeless essence. Yet the dispute may be more useful if it asks what a shared collection enables, whom it excludes, and which obligations follow from its use.

Imagine that the proposed collection begins with equipment residents need occasionally but cannot easily purchase or store. Ownership would leave many tools idle in separate cupboards; lending would make a smaller stock available to more households. This is a reason for the collection, but it is not yet a sufficient defense. A tool available on paper may be practically unavailable to someone unable to collect it during opening hours. A catalog can count objects without recording the obstacles between those objects and their intended users. The number of loans tells us something about use, not everything about access.

Maintenance makes the difference especially visible. A book with a torn cover may remain readable; a damaged ladder can become dangerous. Lending tools therefore creates duties that cannot be discharged by applying every existing rule unchanged. Inspection, clear instruction and a reliable way to report defects become part of the service itself. These duties do not prove that tool lending falls outside the library’s mission. They show why an expanded mission needs expanded practices. The relevant comparison is between plausible versions of the service, not between an idealized new collection and a costless familiar one.

A second objection deserves more weight: a popular tool collection might consume funds needed for books, quiet space or skilled staff. Calling every useful activity a library service would provide no principled way to choose among them. The answer cannot simply be that communities want tools. A proposal must explain how shared access serves the institution’s public purpose and what it would displace. A limited trial with published costs and opportunities for nonusers to respond could reveal tradeoffs that a declaration of mission conceals. Evidence of demand would then be considered alongside evidence about neglected needs.

The institution need not choose between an identity fixed forever and an identity rewritten by each fashionable request. It can treat its mission as a continuing public argument, constrained by resources and responsibilities. On this view, a successful trial would justify retaining a particular service under particular conditions, not demonstrate that libraries should lend every useful object. The drill matters less as a new symbol on the shelf than as a test of whether an institution can revise its practices while remaining answerable to the people it exists to serve.

passage.title: The Archive’s Gaps
passage.contentNote: Original Cortex practice essay and fictional examples. Independent CARS review is pending. This is not an official AAMC item.
passage.text:
An archive often presents itself as a place where the past has been kept. This description is convenient but incomplete. No institution preserves every document, conversation or object, and surviving material does not arrive without a history of selection. The danger is not simply that an archive has gaps. It is that a reader may mistake what happens to have survived for a complete account of what once mattered. An honest archive must therefore preserve ways to question its own boundaries as well as material within them.

Consider a fictional town whose records consist largely of property transactions and council minutes. The collection can support detailed accounts of ownership and formal decisions. It may say much less about the work of residents who owned little property or addressed disputes outside the council chamber. This imbalance does not make the surviving records false. It limits the questions they can answer alone. To discard them because they are partial would lose valuable evidence; to treat them as sufficient would turn a condition of survival into an unwarranted claim about historical importance.

Inviting residents to contribute recorded memories seems an obvious remedy, but it creates new choices rather than abolishing selection. Who hears the invitation? Who has time to respond? Which languages can the institution record and interpret? A collection that adds many interviews may still repeat the exclusions of its earlier holdings. Counting contributions cannot by itself establish that missing experiences are now adequately represented. Nor can a single narrator be made responsible for speaking on behalf of everyone whose circumstances resemble their own. More material can widen inquiry without completing it.

One might object that attention to every omission would leave archivists unable to collect anything. Resources are limited, and selection is unavoidable. The objection succeeds against an impossible demand for completeness, but not against a demand for accountability. An institution can document why it chose a collection, name important limits and make the rationale open to challenge. Such records will not restore every lost voice. They can help later researchers distinguish an absence produced by an explicit collecting rule from an absence whose cause remains uncertain. That distinction changes what can responsibly be inferred.

Transparency itself can become a ritual. A long policy document may satisfy an administrative requirement while remaining inaccessible to the people whose experience it describes. Accountability requires a usable opportunity to question a decision and, where appropriate, alter it. This does not give every objection the force of a veto; competing requests still require judgment. It does require reasons that can be examined rather than assurances that the institution has already considered everything. An archive earns trust less by appearing to contain the whole past than by helping readers understand how its evidence was assembled and how its limits might be revised.

questions.stem: The author’s main recommendation is that archives should:
options: Preserve all available material before permitting historical research.
Replace official documents with oral histories.
Expose collection choices to meaningful challenge and revision.
Avoid judgments about which collections deserve resources.
questions.explanation: The opening and conclusion connect trustworthy evidence to usable accountability for collection boundaries.
optionFeedback: The author rejects completeness as an attainable requirement.
The author preserves the value of official documents and also questions the selection involved in interviews.

The absence of a record proves that an event did not occur.

optionFeedback: Paragraph 2 explicitly separates the truth of surviving records from the range of questions they can answer alone.
No such necessary condition for accuracy is given.
The example warns against turning survival patterns into claims about importance.
The passage cautions against drawing unsupported conclusions from absence.

options: The archive stores interviews in a different room from council minutes.

Some interview transcripts are longer than property records.

optionFeedback: Physical separation is not evidence that the campaign repeats prior exclusion.
The campaign can increase volume without reaching missing perspectives, which is the exact concern in paragraph 3.

Numbering is compatible with either broad or narrow participation.

questions.stem: Which finding would most directly challenge a particular archive’s claim that publishing its policy has had no practical effect?
options: Policy objections regularly produce documented changes in collecting decisions.
The archive’s policy contains several pages of technical vocabulary.
The archive receives few objections after making its form hard to locate.
The archive adds more documents without recording the reasons for selecting them.
questions.explanation: Documented changes resulting from policy objections directly challenge the claim of no practical effect. This does not establish that every archive’s policy works.
optionFeedback: Documented changes resulting from policy objections directly challenge the claim of no practical effect. This does not establish that every archive’s policy works.
Technical vocabulary alone does not establish an effect on decisions.
Few objections under an inaccessible process do not establish practical influence.
More holdings without recorded reasons do not connect any change to the published policy.

options: It necessarily makes all historical inference impossible.
It eliminates the need to preserve incomplete records.
Recorded reasons clarify gaps without filling them.
It requires researchers to agree with every institutional decision.
